title: Sliding Window and Two Pointers
relevance: Sliding window and two pointers are the optimal patterns for many contiguous subarray/substring problems in SDE interviews and OAs, replacing naive enumeration with linear passes.

phases.goal: Establish why sliding window beats naive contiguous enumeration and name the four canonical patterns.

must_hit.point: A naive approach considers all O(N^2) contiguous subarrays; a sliding window with left and right pointers reduces time to O(N).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts all-subarrays enumeration with two-pointer tracking of a valid window and states the O(N^2) to O(N) drop.

must_hit.point: Every sliding window problem falls into one of four patterns: constant/fixed-size, longest/variable, shortest/variable, or counting subarrays.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate lists all four patterns by name without collapsing longest and shortest into one.

must_hit.point: Exactly-k counting uses the atMost trick: subarrays with exactly k equals atMost(k) minus atMost(k-1).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states exactly k as the difference of two at-most sliding-window counts.

must_hit.point: In an atMost sliding window, the number of valid subarrays ending at right is exactly right - left + 1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains counting by adding the count of endings at the current right pointer as right - left + 1.

probes: Why is sliding window preferred over checking every contiguous subarray, and what are the four canonical patterns?
How do you convert an exactly-k subarray count into sliding-window work?

hints.1: Think about what left and right track versus enumerating every pair of endpoints.
hints.2: Name fixed-size, longest, shortest, and counting; for exactly k, relate atMost(k) to atMost(k-1).
hints.3: Naive is O(N^2) contiguous subarrays; window is O(N). Exactly k = atMost(k) - atMost(k-1), and valid endings at right contribute right - left + 1.

phases.goal: Explain expand/shrink rules for each pattern and the key bookkeeping tricks from the worked examples.

must_hit.point: Longest/variable: expand right; while invalid, shrink left until valid again; track the maximum window size seen.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes expand-then-shrink-while-invalid and updating a max length.

must_hit.point: Shortest/variable: expand right until valid, then aggressively shrink left while still valid, tracking the minimum window; update the answer only while the window is valid (inside the shrink loop).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate places the min-answer update inside the while-valid shrink loop, not after every right move.

must_hit.point: Fixed-size window slides by adding the rightmost element and removing the leftmost; Maximum Points from Cards minimizes a leftover middle window of size n - k so total sum minus that min leftover is maximized.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate reframes picking k from ends as minimizing the contiguous leftover of length n - k.

must_hit.point: Longest substring without repeating characters can jump left to last_seen[c] + 1 when a duplicate lies inside the current window, using a last-seen array sized for 256 ASCII characters.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate mentions last-seen indices and jumping left past the prior occurrence rather than only stepping one by one.

must_hit.point: In longest repeating character replacement, replacements needed are window length minus max frequency; max_frequency need not be decremented on shrink because only a higher max_frequency can yield a strictly longer valid window later.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states (window_length) - max_frequency <= k and justifies keeping historical max_freq.

must_hit.point: Minimum window subsequence is a two-pointer forward/back scan, not a standard window, because order matters for a subsequence; after matching s2 forward to right, scan backwards to find the shortest window ending at right, then resume from left + 1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate distinguishes subsequence order from multiset containment and describes forward match then reverse shrink.

probes: Walk through how left and right move for longest versus shortest variable windows.
How does Maximum Points from Cards become a fixed-size window problem?
Why can character-replacement skip decrementing max_freq when shrinking?

hints.1: Separate expand/shrink goals: maximize length, minimize length, or slide a fixed width.
hints.2: For shortest, say when you write down the answer; for cards, what contiguous middle remains; for replacement, what only a larger max_freq could enable.
hints.3: Longest: shrink while invalid, track max. Shortest: shrink while valid and update min inside that loop. Cards: minimize sum of window size n - k. Replacement: keep max_freq without strict downgrade. Subsequence: forward then backward match, not a plain validity window.

phases.goal: Contrast naive enumeration, shrink strategies, and when a standard window is the wrong model.

must_hit.point: Trading O(N^2) enumeration of all contiguous subarrays for an O(N) two-pointer window is the core complexity win when the validity condition can be maintained incrementally.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate ties incremental left/right maintenance to dropping from O(N^2) to O(N).

must_hit.point: Shrinking left one step at a time versus jumping left via last-seen indices: jumping is valid when duplicates invalidate the window and the last occurrence marks the safe new left bound.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains last-seen jump for no-repeat substrings versus while-loop shrink for count-based constraints like at most k zeros.

must_hit.point: Standard sliding window assumes a contiguous validity condition on a multiset of characters; minimum window subsequence needs forward/back two pointers because subsequence order constraints are not captured by a plain window count.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says order matters so after a full forward match you reverse-match to tighten left.

must_hit.point: Fruit Into Baskets (at most 2 distinct) versus Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct Characters share the same longest-window map structure; the specialized case only hard-codes size greater than 2 versus greater than k.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate notes Fruit is Pattern 2 with <= 2 distinct and K-distinct is the same skeleton with parameter k.

probes: When would you jump left with last-seen instead of decrementing a counter in a while loop?
Why is minimum window subsequence not solved like minimum window substring?

hints.1: Compare what invalidates the window: a repeated character versus too many distinct types or unmet needs.
hints.2: Substring containment is about frequencies; subsequence adds order—say what extra scan that forces.
hints.3: No-repeat: jump left to last_seen[c]+1 if inside the window. Count/map constraints: while invalid, step left. Subsequence: forward match then backward tighten; not standard window validity.

phases.goal: Map interview keywords and classic prompts onto the correct pattern and shrink condition.

must_hit.point: Recognize sliding window from keywords like contiguous subarray or substring plus longest/shortest/maximum optimization or a count requirement; the crux is defining the condition that makes the window invalid (the shrink condition).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate cites contiguous/substring cues and insists on stating the shrink/invalid predicate first.

must_hit.point: If asked for exactly K of something, immediately use atMost(K) - atMost(K - 1); Binary Subarrays With Sum, Nice Subarrays (odds as 1/evens as 0), and Subarrays with K Different Integers all follow this.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names the atMost difference and maps at least one of those problems onto it.

must_hit.point: Max Consecutive Ones III reframes as longest subarray with at most k zeros (Pattern 2); expand right counting zeros and shrink left while zeros exceed k.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate restates flip-at-most-k-zeros as longest window with zeros <= k.

must_hit.point: Number of Substrings Containing All Three Characters can count in one O(N) pass with a last-seen map: once all three of 'a','b','c' are seen, add 1 + min of the three last-seen indices for substrings ending at right.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes last-seen of a/b/c and adding 1 + min(last_seen) when all are non-sentinel.

probes: How do you spot a sliding-window OA prompt, and what do you write down before coding?
Given exactly k odd numbers in a subarray, which pattern and formula do you use?
How would you rephrase Max Consecutive Ones III as a window validity condition?

hints.1: Listen for contiguous/substring plus longest, shortest, or count.
hints.2: State the invalid/shrink rule; for exactly k, reach for two atMost calls.
hints.3: Keywords: contiguous subarray/substring + optimize or count; define shrink condition. Exactly K → atMost(K)-atMost(K-1). Ones III → longest window with at most k zeros.

tradeoffs.topic: Naive all contiguous subarrays vs sliding window
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Enumerating every contiguous subarray is O(N^2). When validity can be maintained by moving left and right, a sliding window processes each index a constant number of times for O(N) time.

tradeoffs.topic: Stepwise left shrink vs last-seen jump
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Count- or map-based constraints (at most k zeros, at most k distinct) shrink left in a while loop. For no-repeat substrings, a last-seen index lets you jump left to last_seen[c]+1 when the duplicate is inside the current window.

tradeoffs.topic: Minimum window substring vs minimum window subsequence
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Substring uses Pattern 3 shortest window with need counts and a formed counter. Subsequence needs forward match of s2 then backward scan to tighten left because order matters, then resume from left+1—not a standard multiset window.

tradeoffs.topic: Strict max_freq maintenance vs historical max_freq
tradeoffs.strong_answer: In longest repeating character replacement, needed replacements are window length minus max frequency. You need not decrement max_freq on shrink; only a higher max_freq can produce a strictly longer valid window later.

gotchas.trap: Updating the answer for a shortest-window problem on every right expansion, including when the window is not yet valid.
gotchas.correction: For shortest windows, update the answer only while the window is valid, inside the while loop that shrinks left.

gotchas.trap: Treating exactly-k counting as a single expand/shrink pass without the atMost difference.
gotchas.correction: Compute atMost(k) - atMost(k-1); in atMost, add right - left + 1 for subarrays ending at right, and guard negative goals (e.g., goal < 0 returns 0).

gotchas.trap: Decrementing max_freq when shrinking in character replacement and thinking the algorithm is wrong if you skip it.
gotchas.correction: Keeping the historical max_freq is intentional: only a larger max_freq can unlock a longer valid window.

gotchas.trap: Applying a standard frequency sliding window to minimum window subsequence.
gotchas.correction: Subsequence order matters; use forward match to find right, then reverse match to find the tightest left, then restart from left + 1.

gotchas.trap: Modeling Maximum Points from Cards as an open-ended two-end search without a fixed window.
gotchas.correction: Leave a contiguous middle of exactly n - k cards; minimize that fixed-size window sum and return total sum minus the minimum leftover.
